sections.title: Climate Humanities
sections.description: This graduate seminar introduces students to the field of Climate Humanities, examining climate not only as a scientific phenomenon but also as a cultural, historical, and political idea. Drawing on work by scholars such as Mike Hulme, Jean-Baptiste Fressoz, and Fabien Locher, the course investigates how climate concepts have been created, forgotten, and reinvented across the history of modernity, shaping both environmental knowledge and public understanding. Through interdisciplinary readings in environmental history, science studies, cultural studies, and critical theory, students will explore the histories of climate thought, contemporary climate narratives ranging from IPCC reports to climate fiction and creative media, and the civic possibilities of climate scholarship. Weekly seminars combine brief lectures, student-led discussion, and reflective writing on a private course blog, encouraging analytical, critical, and creative engagement with the material. The course culminates in a conference-style presentation and final research paper, offering students the opportunity to develop original contributions to environmental and humanistic studies.
